final:
In one month, Long-Term Capital Management lost 44 percent of everything it had. Not over a bad year. Not through a slow unraveling. One month. And the firm that lost it was run by some of the most decorated minds in modern finance. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York organized a private rescue meeting to keep the fund from disorderly liquidation. It called one anyway.

In September 1998, William J. McDonough of the New York Fed gathered representatives from fourteen major banks and securities firms on Wall Street and laid out the situation in terms that left little room for interpretation. Its positions were so large, so deeply tied to major Wall Street dealers and counterparties, that an uncontrolled liquidation wouldn't just end the fund. McDonough's warning was specific: a disorderly unwinding could force a "fire sale" that could "cause widespread disruption" in financial markets.

So he pressed them. Not with a government check, not with a federal takeover — with the argument that the people most exposed to the damage were sitting in that room, and a private consortium was preferable to the alternative. On September 23rd, they agreed. Fourteen firms put in $3.625 billion in exchange for a stake that substantially diluted the fund's existing shareholders. The smartest fund in the world had just needed Wall Street to save it from itself.

What Meriwether brought to LTCM wasn't just a trading strategy — it was a culture, transplanted whole from Salomon Brothers, where he'd run the fixed-income arbitrage desk and risen to vice chairman before a Treasury-bond trading scandal ended his tenure there. The scandal cost him Salomon. What it didn't cost him was the model he'd spent years building: a tight partnership of quantitative traders who believed markets could be read like equations, that price was occasionally wrong, and that wrong prices had to eventually correct.

He rebuilt that partnership at LTCM and staffed it with people who could prove it mathematically. Myron Scholes and Robert C. Merton joined as key figures whose quantitative models underpinned LTCM's relative-value trades, while the fund was still running money.

The strategy they ran together was called convergence trading, and its internal logic was clean. Find two securities that should, by any rational measure, price close to each other — a U.S. Treasury bond and a closely related instrument, say — and when the market temporarily misprices one against the other, buy the cheap one and short the expensive one simultaneously. Hold both positions until the gap closes, which the models said it would, and collect the spread. The long position and the short offset each other, leaving the fund exposed not to the direction of the market but only to the size of the gap between two things that were supposed to track each other.

In practice, the gap kept closing, and the returns were striking. Net of fees, LTCM returned 19.9% in 1994. Then 42.8% in 1995. Then 40.8% in 1996. Then 17.1% in 1997. Four consecutive years of gains, in a fund designed to be indifferent to whether stocks rose or fell. The models weren't predicting markets — they were finding mispricings the market itself had already created, and waiting for gravity to do the rest.

The strategy was called market-neutral, and for four years the results made that label look like an understatement.

By the end of 1997, LTCM did something rare: it handed money back, returning roughly two and three-quarter billion dollars of capital to investors.

That decision, made at the peak of the fund's confidence in its own models, compressed the equity base precisely when the leverage ratios were already high — meaning that when 1998 arrived, the cushion between the fund's assets and its obligations was thinner than it might otherwise have been. The return of capital was not a warning sign at the time. In retrospect, it was the moment the structure became most fragile.

The capital supporting LTCM's leveraged positions contracted. Every dollar of equity now had to absorb more of the downside if the models were wrong.

What the 1997 decision quietly revealed was a fault line that would only become visible under stress. Scholes and Merton's quantitative framework was built to exploit pricing anomalies that the models identified across similar securities. What it did not fully account for — what the collapse would later expose as a point of sharp disagreement — was whether those models could hold during the kind of market stress that had no recent precedent to learn from. In 1997, that question felt academic.

So the capital went out the door, the trades stayed open, and the cushion got thinner.

By early 1998, LTCM had accumulated more than $125 billion in borrowed money set against roughly $5 billion in equity. That ratio — about twenty-five dollars borrowed for every dollar the fund actually owned — was the product of two instruments used together: securities repurchase agreements and derivatives, which together let the fund build extraordinary leverage, with major banks extending financing on very favorable terms and, in some cases, little or no initial margin. Goldman Sachs, Merrill Lynch, J.P. Morgan, UBS: major Wall Street dealers were all on the other side of these arrangements.

Why so little resistance? Because the models said the trades were safe. The net exposure, on paper, was small. When a counterparty looked at LTCM's books, the risks seemed to cancel out. What they were not measuring — what the structure made difficult to see — was the scale of what would need to be sold if the canceling stopped.

When UBS wanted exposure to LTCM's returns, it arranged a special transaction specifically designed to get closer to the fund. It would later write off $680 million from that position alone.

That is the turn the models obscured. The leverage wasn't the product of recklessness — it was the logical conclusion of certainty. And the banks kept lending because they believed it too.

On September 2, 1998, John Meriwether sent his investors a letter. Not a quarterly update, not a reassurance — a confession. The fund had suffered, in his own words, "a one-month loss of 44 percent." The firm had been, he wrote, "severely impacted" by the market turmoil, and it was now seeking a capital infusion to survive.

The letter also warned, in language that has been widely quoted, that the firm had been hit by a 'severe liquidity crisis.' The bluntness of that language, coming from Meriwether, was itself a signal of how little room remained.

To understand what produced that number, you have to go back to what the models assumed. Convergence trades were built on a single premise: that gaps between similar securities close. The market turmoil did the opposite. Gaps didn't narrow — they widened. And because LTCM had borrowed heavily across its positions, the damage compounded fast.

Forty-four percent gone in a single month. Then the rest followed. By late September 1998, LTCM had lost about 90% of its capital, and its losses for the year reached about $4.6 billion of its $4.7 billion capital base. What remained was a fund that was, in any practical sense, empty, still sitting on top of massive open positions it could no longer support.

That asymmetry is what made the situation everyone's problem. The losses were LTCM's. The positions were the world's.

McDonough repeated that warning in public testimony. That was not a forecast. By late September, it was an imminent operational question. If the fund collapsed and those positions hit the market at once, the act of selling would crater the prices of the very assets the creditors held. The rescue wasn't charity. It was the creditors protecting themselves from a flood they had helped build.

McDonough's public framing was deliberate: this was a private-sector solution to a private-sector problem. A $3.625 billion recapitalization, spread across fourteen institutions, bought the fund time to unwind its positions in an orderly way rather than all at once. In exchange, the creditors took control of the fund. The partners who had built it, run it, and staked their reputations on it were substantially diluted out of it.

On September 23, 1998, the private-sector parties reached an agreement providing a capital infusion of approximately three-and-a-half billion dollars, the figure McDonough cited publicly, with the precise recapitalization amount recorded as $3.625 billion. The September 23rd agreement came after weeks in which the fund's capital had been nearly entirely consumed, and it arrived not as a preventive measure but as a last available alternative to immediate collapse.

Fourteen institutions joined that rescue, and that number is not incidental. It reflects how widely the financing had been distributed, how many institutions had extended credit on favorable terms, and how many balance sheets were now entangled in the same set of positions.

The models had said the positions were safe because they offset each other. What they could not price was the cost of being forced to sell everything simultaneously into a market with no buyers. That was never a model failure in the abstract. In September 1998, it became a balance sheet.

The exact terms of how that wind-down proceeded — the private negotiations, the internal records, the full accounting of each counterparty's exposure — were settled away from any public regulatory record and remain, in part, disputed or undisclosed. Clearly is that the rescue was organized.

But the question the rescue raised was one the rescue itself could not answer. What it does not resolve is what the Fed's willingness to convene that room, to press those firms, to put its institutional weight behind a consortium rescue — what that signals about where private risk ends and collective exposure begins. LTCM was a private fund. Its models were quantitative. Its leverage was assembled through contracts between consenting institutions. And yet the moment it failed, none of that privacy held. The consequences were everyone's problem.

McDonough's role was to press the assembled banks toward a collective answer, because no individual firm had an incentive to act alone — acting alone meant absorbing costs while others waited. The Fed's institutional weight was what made a room full of competitors behave, for that moment, like a consortium.

The returns were real. The certainty those returns produced was not irrational — it was the logical conclusion of the evidence available. And that certainty justified the leverage. And the leverage made the fund, without anyone announcing it, a risk that extended far beyond the people who had chosen to take it.

It began with a 44 percent loss in a single month, at a fund run by some of the most decorated minds in modern finance. It ended in a room at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, where fourteen banks and securities firms put up $3.625 billion to save it from itself. The models didn't cause it. The certainty did — the certainty that made the leverage feel like precision rather than exposure, until the moment the market stopped cooperating and the only thing left to do was fill a room with creditors and explain, plainly, what they had all built together.
